hints: Notice the diagram shows straight wavefronts with small spacing $\lambda$ arriving at a gap that is much wider than that spacing.
Recall that strong diffraction needs wavelength $\lambda$ to be comparable to the gap width, not much smaller than it.
Check each change for whether it makes $\lambda$ larger relative to the gap width, using $v = f\lambda$ for the ripple tank waves.
walkthrough: Look at the given diagram: plane wavefronts with relatively short wavelength are incident on a wide gap, so only some spreading at the edges is seen.

State the governing rule: significant diffraction is observed when the wavelength $\lambda$ is comparable in size to the gap width, with maximum spreading when $\lambda$ is about equal to the gap width.
Increasing amplitude changes energy and brightness but leaves $\lambda$ and gap width unchanged, so the diffraction pattern shape is unchanged.

For water waves of approximately constant speed, $v = f\lambda$, so increasing frequency $f$ decreases $\lambda$ and increasing the gap width also makes the ratio $\lambda$ to gap width smaller, both giving less spreading.
Increasing the wavelength makes $\lambda$ larger and closer to the gap width, giving more spreading into the region beyond the gap. This is option C.

options.A: Increasing amplitude makes the waves brighter in the ripple tank but does not change the amount of spreading into the shadow region.
options.B: For constant wave speed $v = f\lambda$, increasing $f$ decreases $\lambda$, so $\lambda$ becomes smaller compared with the gap and diffraction is reduced.
options.C: A larger $\lambda$ becomes more comparable to the gap width, so the waves spread out more strongly after the gap.
options.D: A wider gap makes the gap width much larger than $\lambda$, so the waves continue more nearly straight on with less noticeable spreading.
